researchStatement: I develop optimization methods for coordinating interdependent operations and adapting decisions under changing conditions.
biography: I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, working with Angela Kitali. My research examines coordination and adaptation in operations and supply chain systems, with an emphasis on mathematical optimization and AI.

Previously, I was a postdoctoral research scholar at Florida State University, where I received my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering in August 2025 under the supervision of Maxim A. Dulebenets. I received my B.S. in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University in June 2022.
homeResearch: My research investigates how operations and supply chain systems should be coordinated as resources, information and operating conditions change. Decisions made at one stage constrain what is feasible elsewhere; investments made today determine the flexibility available when disruptions occur. I study these interdependencies to understand when integrated planning creates value, how bottlenecks shift, and how that value is distributed across organizations.

Methodologically, I develop mathematical programming formulations and algorithms that combine decomposition, adaptive search and exact optimization. The central challenge is to represent operational interdependencies while keeping the resulting decision problems computationally tractable. My scheduling studies examine how formulation structure and the interaction between search and exact subproblems affect computational performance. A complementary direction examines how learning and language models can assist formulation and search through interaction with mathematical solvers.

Coordination also shapes how systems respond to disruption and adopt new technologies. I am interested in how firms prepare for disruption, how recovery decisions preserve or revise existing commitments, and how electrification and automation alter investment and operating choices. Healthcare, humanitarian logistics and public infrastructure extend these questions to settings where resource allocation directly affects the reliability and accessibility of essential services.
academicContext: My research developed from an engineering interest in transportation systems into a methodological focus on operations research. Following undergraduate study at Wuhan University, I pursued doctoral research at Florida State University on mathematical models and algorithms for interdependent scheduling decisions.

Under the supervision of Maxim A. Dulebenets, my dissertation investigated hyperheuristic algorithms for berth scheduling. Related studies examined cross-docking, ship schedule recovery and infrastructure resource allocation. These problems established a continuing interest in formulation design, adaptive search and the coordination of decisions across an operating system. I also completed a Graduate Certificate in Engineering Data Analytics.

After completing my Ph.D. in August 2025, I continued at Florida State University as a postdoctoral research scholar. I joined the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus in June 2026 to work with Angela Kitali. My current projects include AI-assisted infrastructure inventories, while my broader research develops optimization methods for coordinated, resilient operations.

My project experience includes research supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Department of Transportation. I am a co-principal investigator on the Washington speed-management inventory project. I have taught and assisted with graduate courses in optimization and freight facilities, mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers, and served on an external master’s thesis committee.

How should plans adapt to changing demand, limited capacity and disruption?
How can AI assist optimization while keeping decisions mathematically valid and interpretable?
